questions.q: Why can no single straight line classify all four XOR points correctly?
options: Because the bias $b$ is limited to $[-2.2, 2.2]$
Because $s(1,0) + s(0,1) = s(0,0) + s(1,1)$, so the two positive scores and two negative scores cannot both hold
Because there are too few points to fit a line
Because the points are not on a grid
questions.explain: For $s = w_1 x + w_2 y + b$ both sums equal $w_1 + w_2 + 2b$, yet XOR needs one sum $\ge 0$ and the other $< 0$ — a contradiction. It is geometry, not slider range.

questions.q: What is the smallest number of XOR points that the best single straight line must still get wrong?
questions.explain: Cutting off one corner gets 3 points right; the grid-search button confirms 1 mistake is the best possible.

questions.q: Set the angle to 0° (normal $w = (1, 0)$) and $b = -0.5$, so the rule is "predict + if $x - 0.5 \ge 0$". How many XOR points are misclassified?
questions.explain: Predictions: $(0,0) \to -$ ✓, $(1,0) \to +$ ✓, $(0,1) \to -$ ✗, $(1,1) \to +$ ✗. The vertical line ignores $y$, so it gets 2 wrong.

questions.q: A linear classifier on 2-D data divides the plane into what?
options: Two half-planes separated by one straight line (a hyperplane)
questions.explain: One hyperplane gives exactly two half-spaces — which cannot carve out the inner blob of the ring dataset. Curved or nested boundaries need non-linearity.
